title: JSON
summary: Turn objects into JSON text with JSON.stringify and read JSON text back with JSON.parse.

quiz.code:
const text = JSON.stringify({ name: 'Asha', age: 19 });
console.log(text);
quiz.explain: `JSON.stringify` returns a string. Keys become double-quoted text and there are no extra spaces.
`JSON.parse` turns the text back into a real object, so `data.marks` is an array and index 1 is `90`.

quiz.q: Which of these is valid JSON text?
quiz.explain: JSON is stricter than JavaScript objects: keys and strings need double quotes, and a trailing comma is not allowed.

quiz.q: Click the line that will throw an error.
quiz.explain: The text is not valid JSON because the key `name` has no quotes, so `JSON.parse` throws a SyntaxError on line 2. Wrap risky parsing in `try...catch`.

quiz.q: Complete the call so the JSON text is indented with 2 spaces.
quiz.explain: The third argument sets the indentation. The second one (`null` here) is an optional filter that you can ignore for now.

exercise.task:
In `json.js`, write three functions:

- `parseOrNull(text)` returns the parsed value, or `null` when the text is not valid JSON (use `try...catch`).
- `toPrettyJson(value)` returns the JSON text indented with 2 spaces.
- `copy(value)` returns a deep copy of an object by converting it to JSON text and back, so changing the copy never changes the original.
hints: `JSON.parse` throws when the text is invalid. A `try { ... } catch { ... }` lets you return `null` instead of crashing.
`JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)` gives pretty text. For `copy`, stringify first and then parse the result.
